title: Web: workflows and Experts
summary: The web-build area has five thin App Router pages and five client components (2,713 lines). They cover the workflow list, editor and execution monitor, and the Experts list and editor. Most boundaries are right. The pages are small Server Components that await params and mount one client island. Every successful reply except the three session starts is parsed with the generated api-client parsers, and saves and publishes carry expected versions. The monitor only reads and keeps the last known state through disconnects. The screens also take real care over accessibility and carry why-comments tied to WF-, EX- and Decision IDs. The cost is in how the client components are built. WorkflowEditor (617 lines, 11 state hooks, eight handlers), ExpertEditor (393), WorkflowsPanel (341) and ExpertsPanel (255) each write their own reads, writes, refusal parsing and messages, with no shared read or submit hook. That is where the defects are. Nine create, publish and run calls make a new Idempotency-Key on every click and never disable their buttons, so a double-click on Run this version starts two executions even though the server stores idempotency receipts. Ten reply bodies are cast with type assertions although parseErrorResponse and parseSessionView exist. Six secondary reads fail silently: into Loading text that never clears, into a missing Budget field or Blocks card, or, on the Experts page, into a Read only classification. Rules the server owns are copied into the browser and have started to drift: the offered model profiles, the WF-06 IR version, run-state tones and the terminal set, and budget choices. The editors also have no dirty state, and the workflow editor's two publish buttons publish from different sources. The most valuable changes are these. Add a useResource and useSubmit pair in lib/, starting from the useLoaded hook the tool catalog already has. Split WorkflowEditor around a draft hook, with the IR helpers in a unit-tested lib module. Create one shared module each for model-profile labels, run-state presentation, and money and time formatting.

scores.why: Strict TypeScript and the project lint pass, and the pages are thin Server Components. But DH-06's duplicate-submit, explicit-state and no-assertion rules are missed (9 unguarded keyed writes, 15 assertions, 6 silent reads), and DS-03's radius rule at two sites.

Rules the server owns (offered profiles, WF-06 IR version, run-state tones, budget choices) are copied into components. Shared vocabularies are imported from other screens' component files (run-list, tool-catalog).
Four functions are over 250 lines (WorkflowEditor 617, ExpertEditor 393, WorkflowsPanel 341, ExpertsPanel 255), three files are over 450 lines, and ExpertCard has complexity 27.
Pure helpers are small and well named (withLabel, tidy, expansion, spend). Handlers mix request building, transport, parsing and five-level message ternaries (save has complexity 19).

App Router pages are thin and uniform. Each component file bundles several components, formatting helpers and constants (some declared after use), which keeps pure logic out of reach of the unit harness.

There is no shared read or submit hook. 8 hand-written read effects and 12 writes (9 keyed, 3 unkeyed) each re-implement state, idempotency and messages. Per-click keys defeat server dedupe. The monitor polls every second and reloads all tool uses on each poll.
Comments mostly explain why and cite WF-, EX-, TC- and Decision IDs. One is misplaced, and the body-drain idiom is not explained here.

Successful replies are parsed with generated parsers, except the three session starts, and tsconfig is strict. But error and session bodies, role bindings and a URL parameter are cast (15 assertions), and the IR uses local DraftGraph types.

Refusal codes get clear text. But failed secondary reads look like loading, network and auth failures read as shape errors, contract errors read as reconnecting, and sibling actions map the same code differently.
Browser specs cover the main flows, refusals, conflicts, label IR versions and monitor reconnect. Nothing covers repeated submits or failed secondary reads, and no pure helper has a unit test.
The code is readable, commented and browser-tested. But four oversized components and per-screen copies of fetch, submit, format and rule logic make every change wide and let the copies drift.

strengths.title: Successful replies are parsed with the generated contract
strengths.evidence: These sites pass reply JSON through parse* functions from @autobots/api-client before it reaches state: expert-editor.tsx:83, 102, 160; experts-panel.tsx:40, 50, 116; workflow-editor.tsx:130, 148, 165, 187, 212, 252, 341, 388; workflow-monitor.tsx:52; workflows-panel.tsx:104, 138, 478, 496. Drift on a success path fails at the boundary. The three session starts are the exception (WBLD-03).

strengths.title: Thin Server Component pages with one client island
strengths.evidence: apps/web/app/experts/[id]/page.tsx:8-20, apps/web/app/workflows/[id]/page.tsx:8-20 and apps/web/app/workflow-executions/[id]/page.tsx:8-20 await params, export route metadata and mount one component. apps/web/app/workflows/page.tsx:16-24 wraps the panel that uses useSearchParams in Suspense, with an accessible role=status fallback.

strengths.title: Linkable list state in the URL
strengths.evidence: workflows-panel.tsx:86-89 and 116-124 keep tab, search, selection and version in search params. The tab links use aria-current and scroll={false} (185-189), and key={chosen.id} (380-388) resets the preview when the selection changes, so the view survives reload and Back.

strengths.title: Optimistic concurrency with plain-language conflicts
strengths.evidence: Saves and publishes send expected_version (expert-editor.tsx:143; workflow-editor.tsx:206, 301), and conflicts become clear text (expert-editor.tsx:177-178; workflow-editor.tsx:265-266). experts.spec.ts:104 and workflows.spec.ts:217 exercise this.

strengths.title: Accessibility designed in from the start
strengths.evidence: workflows-panel.tsx:455-467 moves focus to the preview heading and respects reduced motion when it scrolls. Lines 78-79 keep the table usable at 400% zoom, and 230-235 make the scroll region focusable. expert-editor.tsx:339-343 links each disabled tool to its reason with aria-describedby. experts-panel.tsx:373 and 380 give each button and checkbox the Expert's name. workflow-monitor.tsx:178-191 puts words beside every status dot (Decision 0021).

strengths.title: A read-only monitor that cleans up and survives disconnects
strengths.evidence: workflow-monitor.tsx:26 documents that reconnecting cannot start or repeat anything. Line 61 stops polling at a terminal state, 67-70 clear the timer on unmount, and 132-134 keep the last known state while reconnecting. slice-workflows.spec.ts:132-158 drives the disconnect.

strengths.title: Why-comments with traceable IDs
strengths.evidence: workflow-editor.tsx:78-79 explains why nulls are removed (the hash stays stable). Line 89 cites WF-06, 138 cites WF-02, and 144 cites WF-05 and D11. expert-editor.tsx:114-115, 145 and 356 explain what the form keeps or drops. experts-panel.tsx:46 cites EX-02 and EX-03, and workflows-panel.tsx:81-82 cites WF-01, WF-03 and WF-04.

strengths.title: Stable data attributes as test hooks
strengths.evidence: data-field, data-state, data-validation and data-message attributes give the Playwright specs selectors that don't depend on wording or styling, for example expert-editor.tsx:387, workflow-editor.tsx:548 and 568, workflow-monitor.tsx:103 and workflows-panel.tsx:284.

findings.title: WorkflowEditor is one 617-line component that owns eight concerns

locations.note: Component body: 617 lines, complexity 20, 27 statements (ESLint with the review's extra rules)
11 useState hooks: catalog, graph text, validation, message, version, inputs, description, budgets, budget, and so on
One effect loads the workflow, the run-preview budget and the block catalog
Eight async handlers write one shared message slot
Three cards and the block table, inline

findings.impact: Any change to drafts (WF-02), labels (WF-06), budgets (WF-05) or starting an execution edits the same closure, and the concerns leak into each other. For example, saving the description replaces a validation or publish message. No piece can be unit-tested or reused on its own. That is why the editor-state gaps in this review (dirty state, publish sources, duplicate submits) are hard to fix safely here.

findings.title: Create, publish and run calls make a new Idempotency-Key on every click and never disable their buttons

locations.note: run() starts an execution with a new key on every call
Run this version has no pending or disabled state
publish() uses a new key; so does the draft publish at 245
save() uses a new key; so does startSession at 187-199
Save revision and Start a session are never disabled
startRun(); create() at 104-114 and coordinate() at 131-142 do the same
create() uses a new key
The repository's safe pattern: the key stays in a ref until the outcome is known, plus a pending flag

findings.evidence: All nine keyed POSTs build the header inside the handler with "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID(). The sites are expert-editor 140 and 193; experts-panel 89, 111 and 136; workflow-editor 203, 245 and 375; and workflows-panel 133. No trigger in these files is disabled while a request runs. The only disabled props check input: name.trim() === "", routed.size === 0, workflow.draft === null and budgets.length === 0. A lost reply (.catch(() => null)) is reported as a refusal. continue-run.tsx shows the intended shape: it writes "Idempotency-Key": (key.current ??= crypto.randomUUID()), keeps a pending flag, and treats null and 5xx as an unknown outcome.
findings.impact:
The API dedupes by key, through stored receipts in application/experts.py add_version and IdempotencyConflict in api/workflow_routes.py. A new key per click defeats that.
- A double-click on Run this version, or a second press after a lost reply, starts two executions, each with its own budget.
- Start run or Start a session opens two sessions.
- A repeated Save revision or Publish fails the expected-version check and tells the user someone saved a newer version, after their own click.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: 'Disable duplicate submits with server idempotency as the correctness mechanism.' The hook supplies both halves and leaves the server's receipts and version checks as the authority. No guard is weakened.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 9 keyed POSTs with grep and found no trigger disabled while pending; added that a kept key must reset when the body changes, since the server's fingerprint check refuses a reused key with new content.

findings.title: Ten reply bodies are cast although generated parsers exist for them

locations.note: Error body cast
Session reply cast to { id: string }
Session reply cast; also at 144
Error body cast
Error body cast; also at 254, 351 and 392
Error body cast
parseErrorResponse, used 0 times in apps/web
parseSessionView, the schema of the 201 reply to POST /v1/sessions

findings.evidence: Seven refusal reads use: const failure = (await reply?.json().catch(() => null)) as { code?: string; message?: string } | null;. A grep for 'json().catch(() => null)) as' finds 20 such casts in 15 files across the repository. The three session starts read (await reply.json()) as { id: string } and put id into a URL. Every refusal from the API (api/errors.py) and the BFF (lib/bff.ts safeError) has the shape {code, message}, which parseErrorResponse validates. POST /v1/sessions returns SessionView, which parseSessionView validates. parseErrorResponse is used nowhere in apps/web, while every other successful reply in these files is parsed.
findings.impact: DH-06 rules out assertions that hide contract mismatches. If either shape drifts, these paths fail quietly, with generic messages or a push to /sessions/undefined, instead of failing at the boundary like the rest of the screen. The same read-and-cast code is also repeated at each site.
findings.recommendation: Add readRefusal(reply) in lib/. It drains the body and returns parseErrorResponse(...) or null. Use parseSessionView for session starts. Then enable @typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions (assertionStyle: never) for these files as a ratchet.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: explicit response parsing at untrusted boundaries and no blanket assertions. The fix uses the generated parsers and edits no generated file.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 7 refusal casts and 3 session casts in scope; grep finds 20 such casts in 15 files and no parseErrorResponse use in apps/web; every API refusal is built from ErrorResponse (api/errors.py:19-21).

findings.impact: DH-06 and nextjs.md require deliberate loading, unavailable and retryable states. Here a 500 or a dropped connection looks like a load that never finishes. The Experts page presents a safety-relevant classification as known when it isn't (DS-04, state meaning).
findings.recommendation: Promote the useLoaded hook from tool-catalog.tsx:156-181, which already aborts on cleanup, ignores stale replies and returns a typed state, into lib/ as useResource(url, parse). Extend it to return {status: 'loading'|'ready'|'unavailable', data, retry} and to read refused bodies. Render an explicit unavailable line with a Retry control for each secondary read. On the Experts page, treat the classification as unknown until the catalog is ready: disable the two class filters and show 'Checking granted tools'.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: 'Represent loading, empty, denied, unavailable and retryable states deliberately'. nextjs.md: 'explicit error/empty/loading states'. DS-04: state meaning.
findings.verifierNote: All six reads re-read: the code shapes vary (two drain refused bodies) but none has a failed state; the recommendation now builds on the existing useLoaded hook instead of a second new one, and the omitted-budget consequence was added.

findings.title: The editors have no dirty state, and the workflow editor's two publish buttons publish from different sources

locations.note: Editor text, kept apart from the saved WF-02 draft with no comparison between them
Publish sends the textarea and never checks the JSON first
Publish draft publishes the saved server draft, whatever the textarea shows
'Draft saved' shows whenever a server draft exists, even with unsaved edits
Publish and Publish draft sit side by side, with nothing saying what each publishes
publish_draft deletes the draft; publish_version (251) leaves it in place
Save revision is always enabled; Start a session navigates away from unsaved edits

findings.evidence:
The workflow editor holds the IR as one text string (`draft`) next to `workflow.draft` (the saved draft) and the published versions, and never compares them.
- Publish sends graph: parsed(draft) without the parsed(...) === null check that validate() (176-179) and saveDraft() (273-277) apply. Invalid JSON therefore reaches the API as graph: null and returns the generic 'The request is not valid.'
- Publish draft sends only expected_version, so it publishes the stored draft while the textarea may show different, unsaved edits.
- Publishing the textarea leaves an older stored draft in place.
The Expert editor has the same gap. Save revision is always enabled, and each save creates a new version (add_version has no no-op check). Start a session goes to a session bound to the saved version while the edits stay unsaved.
findings.impact: Users can publish or start work from a different graph or configuration than the one on screen, and the badge says 'Draft saved' when the screen isn't. Every fix today has to reason about three implicit states inside a 617-line component.
findings.ruleCheck: Under PRD-Studio WF-02, one saved draft is published under the expected version. The recommendation keeps both publish paths and the server checks, and only makes the browser's view of them explicit (DH-06: browser state is a view of durable state).
findings.verifierNote: Traced both publish paths against publish_draft and publish_version (application/workflows.py:220-303); invalid JSON in publish() reaches the API as graph: null, and add_version has no no-op check.

findings.title: WF-06 IR rules are re-implemented in the browser, and half of the label rule exists only there

locations.note: Local DraftNode and DraftGraph types; parsed(text) is asserted as DraftGraph before it is checked
tidy() strips label: null and ir_version: null, mirroring ir_normalized
withLabel() bumps the graph to ir_version 2, and deletes it when no label is left
draftGraph(draft) is parsed twice per render, then asserted non-null with !
ir_normalized strips null labels and adds ir_version 2 to a labelled graph, but never returns a label-free graph to version 1
Generated WorkflowGraph and WorkflowNode (with label and ir_version), unused here

findings.evidence: The server already canonicalizes every graph it validates, publishes or previews with ir_normalized (api/workflow_routes.py:136, application/workflows.py:58). It drops null labels and a null ir_version, and stores a labelled graph at version 2. The editor repeats this in tidy and withLabel, and adds one rule the server doesn't have: removing the last label deletes ir_version, so the graph returns to version 1 and its old hash. That half runs only when a label input changes. A user who deletes the labels in the JSON textarea keeps "ir_version": 2, and the API stores it. The editor also types the payload with hand-written DraftNode and DraftGraph types instead of the generated WorkflowGraph and WorkflowNode.
findings.impact: WF-06's version rule has two owners that disagree on one case, so a graph's hash depends on which control the user edited. Changing the IR, for example to a version 3, means editing a React component as well as the domain. Each keystroke in a label field also re-serializes the whole graph text, which drops the user's own JSON formatting.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: 'Avoid duplicated business rules'. contracts.md: version the workflow IR. nextjs.md: Next.js owns UI and BFF, not business-state transitions. The recommendation moves ownership toward the domain, edits no generated file, and leaves the hash change to an explicit story. The draft graph is the WorkflowDraftSave payload, so typing it with the generated type uses the DTO without merging it into a view model.
findings.verifierNote: ir_normalized (domain/workflows.py:199-211) keeps an explicit ir_version 2 while withLabel deletes it; re-serialization happens on label edits, not on every keystroke, so that sentence and the nextjs.md wording were corrected. Risk stays high only for the domain story; the interim lib move is low risk.

findings.title: The Expert editor hard-codes which model profiles are offered, and profile labels exist in three copies

locations.note: PROFILES: workspace setting, Terra, Sol
Kept and dropped bindings are computed against PROFILES
The 'not offered for new runs until qualified' option and the dropped-binding notice come from PROFILES

PROFILE_NAMES copy

findings.evidence: PROFILES lists Terra and Sol as the offered choices. Any other saved binding is treated as not offered and removed on save. The server decides the same thing in OFFERED_FOR_NEW_RUNS (domain/models.py:72), which gained Sol on 2026-11-07 under Decision 0019 S2 and S4. It publishes the answer per profile as ModelAvailability.offered through /api/models, which run-disclosure.tsx:47 and model-policy-panel.tsx:136 already read. The labels for ModelProfileId are written out again in experts-panel.tsx and run-list.tsx.
findings.impact: The next change to the offered set needs a matching edit in this component, or the editor misleads. A newly offered DeepSeek would still be labelled 'not offered' and silently dropped from other roles on save. A withdrawn profile would still be offered, and the save would only fail late with model_not_offered.
findings.recommendation: Read /api/models in the editor, or reuse RunDisclosure's read through a shared hook. Build the executor options as model-policy-panel does: the offered profiles plus the current value, marked not offered. Compute kept and dropped from offered. Put the labels in one lib/model-profiles.ts typed Record<ModelProfileId, string>, so a new generated profile breaks the build until it has a label.
findings.ruleCheck: model-gateway.md: three approved profiles, with DeepSeek and Sol offered only once qualified; Decision 0019 S2. The server stays the only owner of 'offered', and no fallback or alternative provider is introduced.
findings.verifierNote: PROFILES at 21-25 and the kept/dropped logic match; OFFERED_FOR_NEW_RUNS is at domain/models.py:72, expert routes call require_offered, and model-policy-panel.tsx:234-235 already builds choices from offered.

findings.title: The execution monitor polls every second with no backoff, reloads all tool uses on each poll, and shows contract errors as reconnecting

locations.note: POLL_MS = 1000, used by the fixed re-poll at 64 with no check of page visibility
A null or 5xx reply sets 'reconnecting' without reading the body; the next poll is still 1 s later
A parse failure (ContractError) also shows as 'reconnecting', indefinitely
loads is incremented on every successful poll, whether or not anything changed
version={loads} drives useToolUses
Each version change re-reads every tool-use page
The run screen follows the same run with an EventSource, a cursor and reconnect
Pins that an unexpected reply reads as reconnecting and that polling recovers to live

findings.evidence: load() (38-65) polls again every POLL_MS = 1000 until the run reaches a terminal state, with no backoff and no visibility check. A null or 5xx reply sets 'reconnecting' without reading the body. A reply that fails parseExecutionView is also shown as 'reconnecting'. slice-workflows.spec.ts:152-166 pins that on purpose: an HTML reply must read as reconnecting, and polling must then recover to live. Nothing tells a ContractError (valid JSON in the wrong shape) apart from a network blip, though. Every successful poll increments loads, and version={loads} makes useToolUses re-read every tool-use page, 200 at a time. run-workspace.tsx:170-204 follows a run with an EventSource, a cursor and a reconnect delay.
findings.impact: While an execution runs, each open monitor, hidden tabs included, sends at least two requests about once a second and downloads the whole tool-use history again, which keeps growing with the run. During an outage it keeps polling every second and leaves refused bodies unread, against the documented drain convention (run-disclosure.tsx:53). After an API or bundle mismatch it shows 'Reconnecting' indefinitely, with nothing that suggests a reload.
findings.ruleCheck: nextjs.md: 'handle reconnect/deduplication and explicit error/empty/loading states. Browser disconnect does not cancel a run.' The monitor stays read-only, as its documented invariant at line 26 requires, and the tested keep-polling behaviour is preserved.
findings.verifierNote: Polling rate, the loads counter and useToolUses' full re-read are confirmed; treating a bad body as reconnecting is pinned by slice-workflows.spec.ts:152-166, so the recommendation now keeps polling and only adds an out-of-date hint for a ContractError.

findings.title: A URL parameter, role bindings and block versions are narrowed without checks

locations.note: params.get('tab') asserted as Tab | null
An unknown tab falls through to the Drafts rule
role_bindings cast to Record<string, string>
The same cast
String(view.block_versions[node_id]) renders 'undefined' for a missing node
checkObject ignores schema-valued additionalProperties
An object without properties becomes Record<string, unknown>

findings.evidence:
Four values are narrowed without a check:
- `const tab = (params.get('tab') as Tab | null) ?? 'all';` accepts any string. inTab then sends an unknown value to the Drafts branch, and no tab has aria-current.
- Two sites cast role_bindings to Record<string, string>. The generator emits Record<string, unknown> for an object without properties, and runtime.ts never checks map values, so the ModelProfileId values are neither typed nor validated.
- The monitor stringifies an unknown map lookup, so a missing key prints 'undefined'.
findings.impact: Each narrowing hides a shape the code then trusts. A hand-edited URL shows the wrong rows, and a binding that isn't a string would be rendered as text or sent back on save.
findings.recommendation: Add isTab() and fall back to 'all'. Read the executor through a typed accessor that calls parseModelProfileId inside try/catch. Render a dash for a missing block version. Fix the root cause in the generator and runtime.ts: emit Record<string, ModelProfileId> and check map values. Never edit generated.ts by hand.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: 'No blanket type assertions'. Ground rule: generated files are regenerated, not edited, so the type gap is fixed in scripts/generate_contracts.py and runtime.ts.
findings.verifierNote: All four narrowings confirmed, with the generator rule at generate_contracts.py:46-47 and checkObject at runtime.ts:64-79; risk raised to medium because the root-cause fix changes generated types and runtime validation for every client.

notCovered:
This was a static reading; no browser session was run. The duplicate-submit, silent-failure and polling-load scenarios are traced from the code, not observed. The claim that unread refusals hold connections open is the repository's own documented rationale (run-disclosure.tsx:53), not something measured here.

Several sources were read only in part:
- Browser specs (experts.spec.ts, workflows.spec.ts, workflow-list.spec.ts, slice-workflows.spec.ts): checked by test titles and grep for route injection, ir_version and double clicks.
- Server files (api/workflow_routes.py, api/errors.py, application/workflows.py, application/experts.py, domain/workflows.py, domain/models.py): read only at the cited lines, to confirm behaviour the web code depends on.
- Sibling web components (run-list, run-disclosure, continue-run, goal-composer, tool-uses, run-workspace, model-policy-panel, ui/card, ui/page-header), the relevant PRD-Development-Harness.md sections (DH-03, DH-06) and the metrics file: read only in part.

Not checked: whether workflow node progress emits run events, which decides whether the monitor can follow the run event stream as run-workspace.tsx does.

Left to the web-architecture lens: whether screens should load first-paint data in Server Components or read it in the browser through the BFF, which is a cross-cutting decision.
